67.original-en: Fred is disturbed by seeing Lydgate gambling and by Farebrother’s warning about his own conduct. He promises to take seriously the chance of a useful life with Mary.

87.original-en: Fred and Mary can look toward a shared home at Stone Court. Their happiness is grounded in the work and trust that have replaced his earlier expectations of an easy inheritance.
87.modern-en: Fred and Mary can look toward a shared home at Stone Court. Their happiness is grounded in the work and trust that have replaced his earlier expectations of an easy inheritance.

88.original-en: Fred becomes a successful farmer and writes on agriculture. His marriage to Mary brings lasting happiness, although his optimism about bargains never entirely disappears.
88.modern-en: Fred becomes a successful farmer and writes on agriculture. His marriage to Mary brings lasting happiness, although his optimism about bargains never entirely disappears.

13.original-en: At Stone Court, Mary answers Rosamond and Fred with plain speech and irony. She refuses to flatter Fred or turn affection into approval of his conduct.
13.modern-en: At Stone Court, Mary answers Rosamond and Fred with plain speech and irony. She refuses to flatter Fred or turn affection into approval of his conduct.

15.original-en: Mary makes clear that Fred must find worthwhile work. She will not encourage him to become a clergyman merely because his family expects it.
15.modern-en: Mary makes clear that Fred must find worthwhile work. She will not encourage him to become a clergyman merely because his family expects it.

26.original-en: Mary learns how Fred’s debt has injured her family. She speaks severely to him while continuing her duties at Stone Court.
26.modern-en: Mary learns how Fred’s debt has injured her family. She speaks severely to him while continuing her duties at Stone Court.

34.original-en: Alone with Featherstone at night, Mary refuses to burn a document at his request without witnesses. She will not accept responsibility for an act whose consequences she cannot know.
34.modern-en: Alone with Featherstone at night, Mary refuses to burn a document at his request without witnesses. She will not accept responsibility for an act whose consequences she cannot know.

41.original-en: Mary’s future work is discussed in the Garth household. Farebrother also hears about her refusal to destroy Featherstone’s will and the worry it has caused her.
41.modern-en: Mary’s future work is discussed in the Garth household. Farebrother also hears about her refusal to destroy Featherstone’s will and the worry it has caused her.

53.original-en: Farebrother relieves Mary’s fear that her refusal to burn the will caused Fred’s loss. She makes clear that Fred must abandon an unsuitable church career and prove himself through work.
53.modern-en: Farebrother relieves Mary’s fear that her refusal to burn the will caused Fred’s loss. She makes clear that Fred must abandon an unsuitable church career and prove himself through work.

58.original-en: Mary and Fred speak at the parsonage. She recognizes Farebrother’s worth but does not let admiration for him erase her attachment to Fred.
58.modern-en: Mary and Fred speak at the parsonage. She recognizes Farebrother’s worth but does not let admiration for him erase her attachment to Fred.

87.original-en: Mary receives the news of Fred’s prospects with joy. Their long attachment can now lead to marriage without requiring her to excuse his former idleness.
87.modern-en: Mary receives the news of Fred’s prospects with joy. Their long attachment can now lead to marriage without requiring her to excuse his former idleness.

88.original-en: Mary and Fred raise three sons at Stone Court. She writes a book for children and remains both affectionate and clear-sighted about her husband.
88.modern-en: Mary and Fred raise three sons at Stone Court. She writes a book for children and remains both affectionate and clear-sighted about her husband.

24.original-en: Caleb has guaranteed Fred’s debt out of trust and affection. His skill in practical work is joined to a dangerous readiness to believe well of people who ask for help.
24.modern-en: Caleb has guaranteed Fred’s debt out of trust and affection. His skill in practical work is joined to a dangerous readiness to believe well of people who ask for help.

25.original-en: Caleb must meet the obligation he guaranteed for Fred. His household bears the cost of his generosity.
25.modern-en: Caleb must meet the obligation he guaranteed for Fred. His household bears the cost of his generosity.

41.original-en: New estate work gives Caleb hope of putting his knowledge of improvements into practice. His restored prospects allow the family to consider keeping Mary at home.
41.modern-en: New estate work gives Caleb hope of putting his knowledge of improvements into practice. His restored prospects allow the family to consider keeping Mary at home.

57.original-en: Caleb sees a possible vocation for Fred and offers to teach him estate work. He makes clear that Mary’s happiness requires seriousness and dependable effort.
57.modern-en: Caleb sees a possible vocation for Fred and offers to teach him estate work. He makes clear that Mary’s happiness requires seriousness and dependable effort.

69.original-en: Caleb considers a plan through which Fred could work at Stone Court. He welcomes the chance without treating an uncertain arrangement as a settled fortune.
69.modern-en: Caleb considers a plan through which Fred could work at Stone Court. He welcomes the chance without treating an uncertain arrangement as a settled fortune.

70.original-en: Caleb brings news of the sick Raffles and withdraws from Bulstrode’s business after hearing accusations against him. He refuses both to continue the connection and to spread the story needlessly.
70.modern-en: Caleb brings news of the sick Raffles and withdraws from Bulstrode’s business after hearing accusations against him. He refuses both to continue the connection and to spread the story needlessly.

87.original-en: Caleb brings the plan for Fred at Stone Court to his family. The opportunity joins Fred’s practical training to a credible prospect of marrying Mary.
87.modern-en: Caleb brings the plan for Fred at Stone Court to his family. The opportunity joins Fred’s practical training to a credible prospect of marrying Mary.

10.original-en: Casaubon introduces Will to Dorothea as his cousin. His drawings and uncertain plans become subjects of conversation, and he resists being measured by a settled profession.
10.modern-en: Casaubon introduces Will to Dorothea as his cousin. His drawings and uncertain plans become subjects of conversation, and he resists being measured by a settled profession.

20.original-en: In Rome, Will and the painter Naumann see Dorothea at the Vatican. Her presence troubles Will more deeply than Naumann’s interest in her as a subject for painting.
20.modern-en: In Rome, Will and the painter Naumann see Dorothea at the Vatican. Her presence troubles Will more deeply than Naumann’s interest in her as a subject for painting.

22.original-en: Will visits Dorothea in Rome and speaks more freely with her. His criticism of Casaubon’s scholarly limitations unsettles her loyalty to her husband.
22.modern-en: Will visits Dorothea in Rome and speaks more freely with her. His criticism of Casaubon’s scholarly limitations unsettles her loyalty to her husband.

23.original-en: Will draws Casaubon into agreeable conversation at dinner and helps arrange a visit to Naumann’s studio. His attention to Dorothea deepens.
23.modern-en: Will draws Casaubon into agreeable conversation at dinner and helps arrange a visit to Naumann’s studio. His attention to Dorothea deepens.

38.original-en: Will discusses work with Mr. Brooke and speaks with Dorothea at Lowick. His wish to remain near her becomes entangled with his search for a useful occupation.
38.modern-en: Will discusses work with Mr. Brooke and speaks with Dorothea at Lowick. His wish to remain near her becomes entangled with his search for a useful occupation.

47.original-en: Will devotes himself to the Pioneer and the reform campaign. In an argument with Lydgate, he defends political action through imperfect people and institutions.
47.modern-en: Will devotes himself to the Pioneer and the reform campaign. In an argument with Lydgate, he defends political action through imperfect people and institutions.

48.original-en: Will goes to church at Lowick hoping to see Dorothea. Casaubon refuses an opening for reconciliation, and Will returns home discouraged.
48.modern-en: Will goes to church at Lowick hoping to see Dorothea. Casaubon refuses an opening for reconciliation, and Will returns home discouraged.

52.original-en: Will watches the collapse of Mr. Brooke’s public performance. He resents the family’s effort to arrange his departure and resolves to leave on his own terms.
52.modern-en: Will watches the collapse of Mr. Brooke’s public performance. He resents the family’s effort to arrange his departure and resolves to leave on his own terms.

55.original-en: Will meets Dorothea but refuses to make a declaration that could appear self-interested. Sir James’s arrival reinforces the obstacles between them.
55.modern-en: Will meets Dorothea but refuses to make a declaration that could appear self-interested. Sir James’s arrival reinforces the obstacles between them.

60.original-en: Rosamond tells Will of the condition in Casaubon’s will. He is humiliated by the suggestion that his attachment to Dorothea can be read as a pursuit of her fortune.
60.modern-en: Rosamond tells Will of the condition in Casaubon’s will. He is humiliated by the suggestion that his attachment to Dorothea can be read as a pursuit of her fortune.

61.original-en: Will angrily rejects Raffles’s approach. The encounter renews his determination not to let the town’s suspicions define his worth.
61.modern-en: Will angrily rejects Raffles’s approach. The encounter renews his determination not to let the town’s suspicions define his worth.

62.original-en: Will learns of Bulstrode’s connection with his family and the money withheld from them. He refuses the offer because accepting it would bind him to a history he finds dishonorable.
62.modern-en: Will learns of Bulstrode’s connection with his family and the money withheld from them. He refuses the offer because accepting it would bind him to a history he finds dishonorable.

63.original-en: Will visits Dorothea before leaving Middlemarch. He tries to convey the depth and constancy of his attachment without seeming to ask her to sacrifice her fortune.
63.modern-en: Will visits Dorothea before leaving Middlemarch. He tries to convey the depth and constancy of his attachment without seeming to ask her to sacrifice her fortune.

79.original-en: Will reproaches Rosamond after Dorothea leaves, making clear that his deepest attachment is to Dorothea. His anger destroys Rosamond’s consoling view of their friendship.
79.modern-en: Will reproaches Rosamond after Dorothea leaves, making clear that his deepest attachment is to Dorothea. His anger destroys Rosamond’s consoling view of their friendship.

80.original-en: Will returns to the house burdened by what has happened. Lydgate’s unsuspecting friendliness makes his position still more painful.
80.modern-en: Will returns to the house burdened by what has happened. Lydgate’s unsuspecting friendliness makes his position still more painful.

83.original-en: Will’s reasons for returning to Middlemarch are reconsidered. Rosamond’s message tells him she has spoken to Dorothea, but he still fears that Dorothea’s trust in him has been damaged.
83.modern-en: Will’s reasons for returning to Middlemarch are reconsidered. Rosamond’s message tells him she has spoken to Dorothea, but he still fears that Dorothea’s trust in him has been damaged.

84.original-en: Will confronts the financial obstacle that has kept him silent. Dorothea’s willingness to renounce the inheritance allows them to choose a future together.
84.modern-en: Will confronts the financial obstacle that has kept him silent. Dorothea’s willingness to renounce the inheritance allows them to choose a future together.

88.original-en: Will enters public life and becomes an ardent reformer in Parliament. His life with Dorothea gradually finds a place within her family’s continuing relationships.
88.modern-en: Will enters public life and becomes an ardent reformer in Parliament. His life with Dorothea gradually finds a place within her family’s continuing relationships.

14.original-en: Bulstrode discusses the hospital and its chaplaincy with Lydgate. Mr. Vincy then asks him to provide the statement Fred needs for Featherstone.
14.modern-en: Bulstrode discusses the hospital and its chaplaincy with Lydgate. Mr. Vincy then asks him to provide the statement Fred needs for Featherstone.

54.original-en: Bulstrode has acquired Stone Court as a prospective retreat. Raffles’s arrival intrudes on those plans and revives fears connected with his earlier life.
54.modern-en: Bulstrode has acquired Stone Court as a prospective retreat. Raffles’s arrival intrudes on those plans and revives fears connected with his earlier life.

62.original-en: The narrator discloses the origins of Bulstrode’s wealth and his concealment of information about his first wife’s daughter. He offers Will money in an effort at restitution.
62.modern-en: The narrator discloses the origins of Bulstrode’s wealth and his concealment of information about his first wife’s daughter. He offers Will money in an effort at restitution.

68.original-en: Bulstrode explains his intention to withdraw from Middlemarch affairs. He refuses Lydgate the personal loan the doctor urgently needs.
68.modern-en: Bulstrode explains his intention to withdraw from Middlemarch affairs. He refuses Lydgate the personal loan the doctor urgently needs.

69.original-en: Bulstrode’s earlier dealings with Raffles explain his wish to leave. He has also discussed letting Stone Court with Caleb, making possible a useful opening for Fred.
69.modern-en: Bulstrode’s earlier dealings with Raffles explain his wish to leave. He has also discussed letting Stone Court with Caleb, making possible a useful opening for Fred.

71.original-en: Bulstrode reverses his refusal and lends Lydgate a thousand pounds. While attending Raffles, he fails to maintain the doctor’s directions about treatment; Raffles dies.
71.modern-en: Bulstrode reverses his refusal and lends Lydgate a thousand pounds. While attending Raffles, he fails to maintain the doctor’s directions about treatment; Raffles dies.

72.original-en: Raffles’s accusations spread through the town. At a public meeting, Bulstrode is challenged about his past and leaves in visible distress.
72.modern-en: Raffles’s accusations spread through the town. At a public meeting, Bulstrode is challenged about his past and leaves in visible distress.

75.original-en: Bulstrode receives Harriet’s companionship without being able to claim innocence. Their shared tears acknowledge a suffering that neither can yet put into words.
75.modern-en: Bulstrode receives Harriet’s companionship without being able to claim innocence. Their shared tears acknowledge a suffering that neither can yet put into words.

86.original-en: Bulstrode agrees to an arrangement for Fred at Stone Court and suggests that Harriet conduct it through Caleb. He recognizes that Caleb will not resume dealings with him directly.
86.modern-en: Bulstrode agrees to an arrangement for Fred at Stone Court and suggests that Harriet conduct it through Caleb. He recognizes that Caleb will not resume dealings with him directly.

75.original-en: Harriet learns the disgrace surrounding her husband. After confronting the knowledge alone, she puts aside her finery and sits beside him in silent loyalty.
75.modern-en: Harriet learns the disgrace surrounding her husband. After confronting the knowledge alone, she puts aside her finery and sits beside him in silent loyalty.

86.original-en: Harriet asks her husband to make amends to her family by helping Fred. She accepts the task of approaching Caleb about Stone Court.
86.modern-en: Harriet asks her husband to make amends to her family by helping Fred. She accepts the task of approaching Caleb about Stone Court.

18.original-en: Farebrother welcomes Lydgate into the household he shares with his mother, aunt and sister. He speaks frankly about his limited income and his wish for the hospital appointment.
18.modern-en: Farebrother welcomes Lydgate into the household he shares with his mother, aunt and sister. He speaks frankly about his limited income and his wish for the hospital appointment.

19.original-en: Farebrother loses the chaplaincy but continues to treat Lydgate as a friend. His generosity makes the doctor’s decision harder to dismiss as a merely practical matter.
19.modern-en: Farebrother loses the chaplaincy but continues to treat Lydgate as a friend. His generosity makes the doctor’s decision harder to dismiss as a merely practical matter.

53.original-en: Farebrother receives the Lowick living and undertakes Fred’s request to speak to Mary. Despite his own feelings, he faithfully helps his younger rival.
53.modern-en: Farebrother receives the Lowick living and undertakes Fred’s request to speak to Mary. Despite his own feelings, he faithfully helps his younger rival.

64.original-en: Farebrother hears reports of Lydgate’s financial difficulties and tries to offer friendly help. The doctor’s guarded reaction prevents the conversation from bringing relief.
64.modern-en: Farebrother hears reports of Lydgate’s financial difficulties and tries to offer friendly help. The doctor’s guarded reaction prevents the conversation from bringing relief.

67.original-en: Farebrother draws Fred away from the Green Dragon and warns him against gambling. He admits his own interest in Mary while making clear that he wants Fred to deserve her.
67.modern-en: Farebrother draws Fred away from the Green Dragon and warns him against gambling. He admits his own interest in Mary while making clear that he wants Fred to deserve her.

4.original-en: Sir James encourages Dorothea’s cottage plans and hopes to please her. She understands his practical help without recognizing his hopes of marrying her.
4.modern-en: Sir James encourages Dorothea’s cottage plans and hopes to please her. She understands his practical help without recognizing his hopes of marrying her.

7.original-en: Mrs. Cadwallader tells Sir James of Dorothea’s engagement. He is distressed by her choice, but begins to pay more attention to Celia.
7.modern-en: Mrs. Cadwallader tells Sir James of Dorothea’s engagement. He is distressed by her choice, but begins to pay more attention to Celia.

9.original-en: Sir James tries to enlist Mr. Cadwallader against the marriage. As he accepts Dorothea’s decision, he finds a less anxious friendship with her and increasingly attends to Celia.
9.modern-en: Sir James tries to enlist Mr. Cadwallader against the marriage. As he accepts Dorothea’s decision, he finds a less anxious friendship with her and increasingly attends to Celia.

39.original-en: Sir James worries about Mr. Brooke’s political ambitions and the condition of his estate. He seeks the Cadwalladers’ help in pressing for practical improvements.
39.modern-en: Sir James worries about Mr. Brooke’s political ambitions and the condition of his estate. He seeks the Cadwalladers’ help in pressing for practical improvements.

50.original-en: Sir James learns that Casaubon’s will penalizes Dorothea if she marries Will. He wants to protect her from the insult and prevent further contact between them.
50.modern-en: Sir James learns that Casaubon’s will penalizes Dorothea if she marries Will. He wants to protect her from the insult and prevent further contact between them.

85.original-en: Sir James reacts angrily to Dorothea’s decision. His disapproval reflects both affection for her and the family’s judgment of Will’s social standing.
85.modern-en: Sir James reacts angrily to Dorothea’s decision. His disapproval reflects both affection for her and the family’s judgment of Will’s social standing.

42.original-en: Raffles visits Joshua Rigg and presses an unwelcome claim on him. Rigg’s rebuke identifies Raffles as the stepfather who mistreated him and his mother.
42.modern-en: Raffles visits Joshua Rigg and presses an unwelcome claim on him. Rigg’s rebuke identifies Raffles as the stepfather who mistreated him and his mother.

54.original-en: Raffles finds Bulstrode and treats their former acquaintance as a source of advantage. His departure does not remove the banker’s fear that he will return.
54.modern-en: Raffles finds Bulstrode and treats their former acquaintance as a source of advantage. His departure does not remove the banker’s fear that he will return.

61.original-en: At the auction Raffles recognizes Will’s name and claims knowledge of his family. He intrudes with information Will has not asked to receive.
61.modern-en: At the auction Raffles recognizes Will’s name and claims knowledge of his family. He intrudes with information Will has not asked to receive.

71.original-en: Raffles dies at Stone Court after a night in which Lydgate’s treatment instructions have not been followed. His death leaves the consequences of his disclosures in other people’s hands.
71.modern-en: Raffles dies at Stone Court after a night in which Lydgate’s treatment instructions have not been followed. His death leaves the consequences of his disclosures in other people’s hands.

13.original-en: Featherstone demands proof that Fred has not borrowed against an expected inheritance. His suspicions give him another means of controlling the young man.
13.modern-en: Featherstone demands proof that Fred has not borrowed against an expected inheritance. His suspicions give him another means of controlling the young man.

33.original-en: Featherstone’s declining health draws his relatives to Stone Court. Their displays of concern are entangled with calculations about his will.
33.modern-en: Featherstone’s declining health draws his relatives to Stone Court. Their displays of concern are entangled with calculations about his will.

34.original-en: Featherstone tries to persuade Mary to destroy one of his wills. She refuses, and by morning he is dead.
34.modern-en: Featherstone tries to persuade Mary to destroy one of his wills. She refuses, and by morning he is dead.

5.original-en: Mr. Brooke tells Dorothea that Casaubon wishes to marry her. His cautious objections do little to disturb her conviction that the marriage will give her life a purpose.
5.modern-en: Mr. Brooke tells Dorothea that Casaubon wishes to marry her. His cautious objections do little to disturb her conviction that the marriage will give her life a purpose.

7.original-en: Mr. Brooke faces Mrs. Cadwallader’s objections to the engagement and explains that Dorothea has made her own choice.
7.modern-en: Mr. Brooke faces Mrs. Cadwallader’s objections to the engagement and explains that Dorothea has made her own choice.

31.original-en: Mr. Brooke invites Will to stay with him. He enjoys the prospect of the young man’s company without fully considering the tensions surrounding the invitation.
31.modern-en: Mr. Brooke invites Will to stay with him. He enjoys the prospect of the young man’s company without fully considering the tensions surrounding the invitation.

39.original-en: Mr. Brooke’s reforming politics invite scrutiny of his own treatment of tenants. His friends find that discussing improvements can feed his appetite for politics rather than restrain it.
39.modern-en: Mr. Brooke’s reforming politics invite scrutiny of his own treatment of tenants. His friends find that discussing improvements can feed his appetite for politics rather than restrain it.

40.original-en: Mr. Brooke attempts to deal kindly with Dagley over the tenant’s son. Dagley’s anger exposes how little the landlord’s benevolent self-image answers the family’s hardship.
40.modern-en: Mr. Brooke attempts to deal kindly with Dagley over the tenant’s son. Dagley’s anger exposes how little the landlord’s benevolent self-image answers the family’s hardship.

50.original-en: Mr. Brooke discusses the will with Sir James but remains occupied with his parliamentary prospects. His handling of Will is affected by both family pressure and political convenience.
50.modern-en: Mr. Brooke discusses the will with Sir James but remains occupied with his parliamentary prospects. His handling of Will is affected by both family pressure and political convenience.

52.original-en: Mr. Brooke’s election speech is mocked by the crowd. The humiliation weakens his political enterprise and changes the prospects of Will’s employment.
52.modern-en: Mr. Brooke’s election speech is mocked by the crowd. The humiliation weakens his political enterprise and changes the prospects of Will’s employment.

25.original-en: Susan confronts the effect of Fred’s default on the family’s savings and plans for their children. Her anger comes from knowing what their limited money was meant to accomplish.
25.modern-en: Susan confronts the effect of Fred’s default on the family’s savings and plans for their children. Her anger comes from knowing what their limited money was meant to accomplish.

58.original-en: Susan’s guarded response to Fred exposes her knowledge of Farebrother’s interest in Mary. An awkward conversation leaves Fred painfully aware of his rival.
58.modern-en: Susan’s guarded response to Fred exposes her knowledge of Farebrother’s interest in Mary. An awkward conversation leaves Fred painfully aware of his rival.

14.original-en: Mr. Vincy presses his brother-in-law to help Fred. The conversation exposes differences between his easy social habits and Bulstrode’s religious discipline.
14.modern-en: Mr. Vincy presses his brother-in-law to help Fred. The conversation exposes differences between his easy social habits and Bulstrode’s religious discipline.

37.original-en: Disappointed by Featherstone’s will, Mr. Vincy reconsiders the family’s expenses and Rosamond’s marriage. The loss of Fred’s expectations changes his view of their prospects.
37.modern-en: Disappointed by Featherstone’s will, Mr. Vincy reconsiders the family’s expenses and Rosamond’s marriage. The loss of Fred’s expectations changes his view of their prospects.

12.original-en: Mrs. Vincy presides over a comfortable household and indulges Fred. The family’s connections with Featherstone and Bulstrode help sustain its sense of consequence.
12.modern-en: Mrs. Vincy presides over a comfortable household and indulges Fred. The family’s connections with Featherstone and Bulstrode help sustain its sense of consequence.

11.original-en: Sir James’s mother discusses health and calls for an introduction to Lydgate. His respectful answers leave her with a favorable opinion of the new doctor.
11.modern-en: Sir James’s mother discusses health and calls for an introduction to Lydgate. His respectful answers leave her with a favorable opinion of the new doctor.

56.original-en: The older Lady Chettam insists on the proper period of mourning and recounts an alarming example of remarriage. Her warnings are addressed to Dorothea as well as the company.
56.modern-en: The older Lady Chettam insists on the proper period of mourning and recounts an alarming example of remarriage. Her warnings are addressed to Dorothea as well as the company.

36.original-en: Rigg appears among Featherstone’s mourners. The reading of the later will makes him heir to the property and requires him to take the Featherstone name.
36.modern-en: Rigg appears among Featherstone’s mourners. The reading of the later will makes him heir to the property and requires him to take the Featherstone name.

42.original-en: Rigg refuses Raffles further support and orders him away. He insists that his mother’s allowance must not become another source of money for her husband.
42.modern-en: Rigg refuses Raffles further support and orders him away. He insists that his mother’s allowance must not become another source of money for her husband.

epithet.en: The religious reformer recalled in the Prelude

1.original-en: The Prelude recalls Theresa’s childhood desire for martyrdom and her later reform of a religious order. It contrasts her recognized achievement with the obscure lives of women whose equally ardent purposes find no public expression.
1.modern-en: The Prelude recalls Theresa’s childhood desire for martyrdom and her later reform of a religious order. It contrasts her recognized achievement with the obscure lives of women whose equally ardent purposes find no public expression.
